source.title: Jailbreaking LLMs with Arabic Transliteration and Arabizi
source.authors: Mansour Al Ghanim; Saleh Almohaimeed; Meng Zheng; Yan Solihin; Qian Lou

record.tranche_reason: Tests jailbreak interventions and harmful-compliance outcomes in Arabic, transliteration, and Arabizi, extending jailbreak findings to a new language setting.
record.gate_note: The study measures harmful-answer rates for Arabic forms and prompt perturbations, including prefix injection and a prefix-plus-suffix attack. It does not test fine-tuning, per-token KL, safety localization in parameters, or training that deepens safety. The system-prompt mitigation results are not rows for the tested bypass interventions. Cited results from other papers are excluded.
record.test_reason: Only the prefix-injection arm (R4, R11) and the prefix-plus-suffix arm (R18, R19, R25) bear on V4. These test a compliant-start prompt and an added suffix on GPT-4 and Claude-3 in Arabic, a new setting. The main transliteration and chatspeak results are an input-encoding attack. They are not getting past the opening, so they fit no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that standardized Arabic is robust even with prefix injection, while transliteration and chatspeak jailbreak GPT-4 and Claude-3. Manual word- and sentence-level perturbations can elicit unsafe output. A conversion/translation system prompt cut GPT-4 transliteration unsafe outputs from 12.12% to 0.77%. They argue that cross-lingual adversarial training is needed.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses Arabic-language forms and prompt perturbations to test jailbreak behaviour; it does not reproduce the original fine-tuning or token-position measurement methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by model, Arabic form, perturbation type, and prompt group. The authors also vary temperature and top-p for error margins in Figure 2.

fits_no_version.finding: Rendering AdvBench in Arabic transliteration or chatspeak raises unsafe rates relative to standardized Arabic. GPT-4 rises 2.50% to 12.12% and Claude-3 0.19% to 4.62%, with large misunderstanding and translation shares.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal fails to generalize to non-standard scripts or encodings of a language (mismatched generalization).

fits_no_version.finding: Small character or word perturbations of previously refused prompts elicit unsafe output, especially for prompts that trigger spurious Google or copyright refusals.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal keyed to surface word forms can be evaded by meaning-preserving perturbations.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, 2024
record.problems: Outputs were manually categorized; the text reports two annotators reaching consensus but gives no inter-annotator reliability measure. Misunderstanding and translation outputs complicate interpretation of unsafe rates. The tested closed-source models and Arabic forms do not establish results for other models or languages.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant numeric results left out. Figure examples that duplicate the aggregate or specific prompt-perturbation results are not entered separately except for the prefix-plus-suffix example in Figure 5.

untested.parts: No per-token KL or position analysis.
Not tested: true assistant-turn prefilling, decoding changes, optimized adversarial suffixes, and any V4 manipulation on open models (Llama2 got no prefix or suffix test).
Shortcut-learning and filter explanations are hypotheses only, not about why safety is shallow.
No deepening training; the mitigation tested is a system prompt.

missing.what: Qualitative chat-interface prefix-injection tests in which GPT-4 and Claude-3 kept refusing (bomb prompts and additional prompts). This is the main basis of the authors' 'not effective' claim.
Error margins across two temperature/top_p runs for the Table 2 conditions, including Arabic-w-prefix.

record.verdict_notes: Most rows test encoding attacks, not getting past the opening, and were relinked to none. R1 value and R2 baseline were corrected: GPT-4 English unsafe is 0.38%. The 'prefix injection' here is text appended to the user message, not a prefilled assistant turn, which weakens its bearing on V4. Manual two-annotator labels are given without a reliability measure.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful-example fine-tuning and its effect on safety are not tested.
Benign-data fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance are not tested.
The study does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL or response-position concentration.

Tests Arabic prefix injection, language-form changes, word and sentence perturbations, and one prefix-plus-suffix attack. It does not test decoding changes or systematic variation of compliant prefilled response tokens.
No parameter or rank localization is tested.
The study offers hypotheses about language-form vulnerabilities but does not test why safety behaviour is shallow or a data/objective explanation for shallowness.
No training to deepen safety across response positions is tested.
